title: SYNCOPE: The Ophthalmic Surgeon's Guide to TLOC
summary: A comprehensive deep dive into Transient Loss of Consciousness (TLOC). This guide bridges Internal Medicine and Emergency protocols with Ophthalmic-specific triggers like the Oculocardiac Reflex, ensuring rapid triage and evidence-based management in the clinic or OR.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Syncope is defined as a transient loss of consciousness (TLOC) due to global cerebral hypoperfusion, characterized by rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous, complete recovery. It must be differentiated from other causes of TLOC such as seizures or metabolic disturbances where blood flow to the brain is maintained.

branches: 5-10 seconds of cessation of blood flow
Decreased Cardiac Output (CO = SV x HR)

rows: AV Block, Brugada, Aortic Stenosis, HOCM, Long QT

sections.title: Ophthalmic-Specific Triggers
content: Intravitreal Injections: Anxiety and pain trigger reflex syncope.
Oculocardiac Reflex (Aschner Reflex): Pressure on globe or traction on extraocular muscles.
Applanation Tonometry: Contact-induced vasovagal response in sensitive patients.
Retrobulbar/Peribulbar Blocks: Sudden increase in orbital pressure.
Laser Procedures: Strong visual stimuli or pain during PRP.

sections.title: The Oculocardiac Reflex (OCR)
content: Step 1: Afferent stimulus via Long and Short Ciliary Nerves.
Step 2: Signal travels to Ciliary Ganglion and Ophthalmic Division of Trigeminal Nerve (V1).
Step 3: Synapse at Sensory Nucleus of Trigeminal Nerve near the Floor of 4th Ventricle.
Step 4: Efferent signal via Vagus Nerve (X) to Sinoatrial (SA) node.
Step 5: Clinical Result: Bradycardia, Arrhythmia, or Cardiac Arrest.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: High-Risk Features
content: Syncope while supine or during exercise
Family history of sudden cardiac death at young age (<40 yrs)
New onset chest pain or dyspnea preceding TLOC
Palpitations immediately followed by syncope
Presence of structural heart disease (HF, low EF)
ECG findings: Brugada pattern, QT prolongation (>450ms), Bifascicular block

sections.title: The Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Thorough History: Prodrome (nausea/warmth) suggests vasovagal; sudden onset suggests cardiac.
2. Physical Exam: Orthostatic vitals (3-min stand test) and cardiac auscultation.
3. 12-Lead ECG: Mandatory for ALL patients to rule out conduction delay.
4. Carotid Sinus Massage: If >40 years and etiology unknown (Caution: check for bruits first).
5. Echocardiogram: If structural heart disease is suspected.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Not All TLOC is Syncope

branches: Cataplexy (Triggered by emotion, no loss of consciousness)

sections.title: Risk Stratification: San Francisco Syncope Rule

content.explanation: C: Congestive Heart Failure; H: Hematocrit < 30%; E: ECG abnormalities; S: Shortness of breath; S: Systolic BP < 90 mmHg. Any positive = High risk for serious outcome.

sections.title: Acute Management Protocol (In-Clinic)
content: 1. Safety: Lay patient supine, elevate legs (Trendelenburg position).
2. Assessment: Check ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) and Glucose.
3. Ocular Check: If OCR suspected, stop ocular manipulation immediately.
4. Recovery: Monitor for 15-30 mins; if cardiac features present, activate EMS.
5. Fluid Resuscitation: Oral fluids if conscious; IV Saline if hypotensive.

sections.title: Pharmacological Considerations
content: Midodrine: Alpha-1 agonist for refractory orthostatic hypotension (2.5-10mg TID).
Fludrocortisone: Mineralocorticoid to expand plasma volume (0.1-0.2mg QD).
Beta-Blockers: Controversial; may help in hyperadrenergic vasovagal syncope.
Atropine: 0.5mg IV for symptomatic bradycardia during Oculocardiac Reflex.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Ophthalmologists
content: Always check a glucose level in diabetic patients who faint in the waiting room.
Patients with 'graying out' of vision (Amaurosis Fugax) may be pre-syncopal due to orthostatic drop.
If a patient faints during a slit-lamp exam, be careful of head trauma against the frame.
Documentation: Note the presence/absence of a prodrome, duration of TLOC, and vitals upon recovery.
The 'Eyes Open' sign: During true syncope, eyes are usually open; closed eyes strongly suggest psychogenic causes.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: Evidence Base
sections.content: The POST (Prevention of Syncope Trial) series demonstrated that fludrocortisone and physical counter-maneuvers (leg crossing, limb tensing) significantly reduce recurrence in reflex syncope. The ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 Guidelines emphasize that a 12-lead ECG is the single most important initial test with the highest diagnostic yield.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Breath-holding spells: Common TLOC mimic in toddlers (6mo - 2yrs).
Long QT Syndrome: May first manifest as 'seizure' during exercise or startle.
Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS): Common in adolescents; HR increase >40bpm without BP drop.
